cues.text: The Chapel of the Holy Cross in Avignon, France, was home to a Franciscan confraternity known as the Gray Penitents.
By the time of the events of 1433, it had maintained perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for some two hundred years.
This devotion traced back to a solemn act of reparation organized by King Louis VIII after his victory over the Albigensian heretics, who had denied the Real Presence.

After days of relentless rain in late November 1433, the Sorgue and Rhone rivers rose to a dangerous height and finally broke their banks, flooding the low-lying chapel, which stood directly along the Sorgue's course.

Convinced that the small church, and the Host exposed within it for adoration, must have been swept away entirely, the head of the confraternity and another friar set out by rowboat to reach the site.
A Dry Path to the Altar
Reaching the chapel proved difficult through the floodwaters.
When the two friars finally arrived and made their way inside, they found the water risen to some four feet throughout the building.
Around the altar itself, however, the floodwater had parted to either side, leaving the altar and the monstrance holding the Host completely dry.
A Song for the Parting Waters
News of what the friars had found spread rapidly through the city, and crowds gathered at the chapel to witness the scene for themselves, several hundred people by the accounts that survive.

In gratitude, the confraternity established an annual commemoration on November 30, the feast of St. Andrew, at which the brothers still sing, before Benediction, verses from the Canticle of Moses composed after the parting of the Red Sea.
The Avignon account belongs to a small category of Eucharistic tradition built not around blood or transformation, but around simple, physical preservation.
The Host and the ground immediately around it were spared from a flood that reached everything else in the building.

Nearly six centuries later, the Gray Penitents still gather each November 30 at the Chapelle des Penitents Gris to mark the anniversary, carrying forward a devotion that has, by their own telling, already survived one flood it should not have.
